content: Dipyridamole can be administered without restrictions as long as there is no evidence of hepatic failure. No studies have been conducted to evaluate the pharmacokinetics of aspirin/dipyridamole in patients with renal dysfunction. However, in the ESPS2 study, patients with creatinine clearances ranging from approximately 15 mL/min to over 100 mL/min showed no changes in the pharmacokinetics of dipyridamole or its glucuronide metabolite when data were adjusted for age differences. The peak plasma concentration of aspirin at steady-state, following administration of a 50 mg daily dose of aspirin (as part of aspirin/dipyridamole 25 mg BID), is 319 ng/mL (range: 175–463 ng/mL). Aspirin undergoes moderate hydrolysis to salicylic acid in the liver and gastrointestinal wall, with 50–75% of the administered dose reaching systemic circulation as intact aspirin. When aspirin/dipyridamole capsules are taken with a high-fat meal, there is no difference in the area under the curve (AUC) for aspirin at steady-state. Although the maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) decreases by approximately 50%, this reduction is not considered clinically relevant due to a similar degree of cyclooxygenase inhibition in both fed and fasted states. Aspirin is poorly bound to plasma proteins, with a low apparent volume of distribution (10 L). Its metabolite, salicylic acid, is highly bound to plasma proteins, but this binding is concentration-dependent and nonlinear. At low concentrations (<100 µg/mL), approximately 90% of salicylic acid is bound to albumin. Salicylic acid is widely distributed throughout the body, including the central nervous system, breast milk, and fetal tissues. Early signs of salicylate overdose, such as tinnitus (ringing in the ears), occur at plasma concentrations of approximately 200 µg/mL. Aspirin is rapidly hydrolyzed in plasma to salicylic acid, with a half-life of 20 minutes. Salicylic acid is primarily conjugated in the liver to form salicyluric acid, phenolic glucuronide, acyl glucuronide, and minor metabolites. Salicylate metabolism is saturable, and total body clearance decreases at higher serum concentrations due to the liver's limited capacity to form salicyluric acid and phenolic glucuronide. Following toxic doses (10–20 g), the plasma half-life of salicylates may increase to over 20 hours. At therapeutic doses, the elimination half-life is approximately 2–3 hours. Renal excretion of unchanged salicylate depends on urinary pH. At a urinary pH of 8, renal clearance of free salicylate increases by 80%. Alkalinization of urine is a key concept in managing salicylate overdose. Following therapeutic doses, approximately 10% of the drug is excreted as salicylic acid and 75% as salicyluric acid, phenolic glucuronides, and acyl glucuronides in urine. Aspirin should be avoided in patients with severe hepatic insufficiency. Similarly, it should not be used in patients with severe renal failure (glomerular filtration rate <10 mL/min). A dedicated drug interaction study in 60 healthy volunteers evaluated the effects of omeprazole (80 mg once daily) on the pharmacokinetics of dipyridamole and the pharmacodynamics of acetylsalicylic acid when co-administered with aspirin/dipyridamole twice daily. Dipyridamole exposure (Cmax and AUC) at steady-state was similar with or without omeprazole co-administration. The pharmacokinetics of acetylsalicylic acid were not characterized, but antiplatelet activity, as measured by arachidonic acid-induced platelet aggregation, was similar between treatment arms at steady-state. In nonclinical toxicology studies, dipyridamole showed no evidence of carcinogenicity when administered in the feed to mice (up to 111 weeks) and rats (up to 128 weeks in males and 142 weeks in females). The highest dose tested (75 mg/kg/day) was approximately equivalent to the maximum recommended human daily oral dose (MRHD) in mice and about twice the MRHD in rats on a mg/m² basis. Combinations of dipyridamole and aspirin (1:5 ratio) tested negative in the Ames test, in vivo chromosome aberration tests (in mice and hamsters), oral micronucleus tests (in mice and hamsters), and oral dominant lethal tests (in mice). Aspirin alone induced chromosome aberrations in cultured human fibroblasts. Mutagenicity tests of dipyridamole alone in bacterial and mammalian cell systems were negative. The effects of dipyridamole and aspirin combinations on fertility and reproductive performance have not been evaluated. However, no evidence of impaired fertility was observed when dipyridamole was administered to male and female rats at oral doses up to 500 mg/kg/day (approximately 12 times the MRHD on a mg/m² basis). A significant reduction in the number of corpora lutea, implantations, and live fetuses was observed at doses of 1250 mg/kg/day (more than 30 times the MRHD on a mg/m² basis). Aspirin inhibits ovulation in rats.
